# Introduction

Large sparse matrices, such as single-cell counts, are often stored in
[Zarr](https://zarr.dev) stores. AnnData's `write_zarr()` saves its `X`
matrix in a Zarr group as three 1D arrays:

- `data`: the nonzero values
- `indices`: the 0-based column (CSR) or row (CSC) index of each value
- `indptr`: where each row (CSR) or column (CSC) starts in `data` and
  `indices`

`ZarrSparseMatrix` represents such a matrix in R without loading it into
memory. It is a `DelayedMatrix`, so it works with any code written for
`r Biocpkg("DelayedArray")` objects, and it is the Zarr counterpart of
`HDF5Array::H5SparseMatrix`. Data is read with `r Biocpkg("Rarr")` only when
it is needed. Selecting rows of a CSR matrix, or columns of a CSC matrix,
reads only the corresponding parts of `data` and `indices`.

# Installation

```{r install, eval=FALSE}
if (!requireNamespace("BiocManager", quietly=TRUE))
    install.packages("BiocManager")

# Install from Bioconductor
BiocManager::install("ZarrSparseMatrix")

# Install from GitHub
# remotes::install_github("GabrielHoffman/ZarrSparseMatrix")
```

# Creating a ZarrSparseMatrix

The package includes a small example store: simulated counts for 200 cells
and 100 genes, stored like AnnData's `X` (CSR layout, cells as rows).
`exampleZarr()` unzips it to a temporary directory and returns its path.

```{r load}
suppressMessages({
library(ZarrSparseMatrix)
})

store <- exampleZarr()
store
list.files(store, recursive=TRUE, all.files=TRUE)[1:6]
```

Pass the path to the store and the name of the group:

```{r construct}
X <- ZarrSparseMatrix(store, "X")
X
```

The dimensions and layout come from the group's `shape` and `encoding-type`
attributes:

```{r attrs}
dim(X)
type(X)
is_sparse(X)
seed(X)
```

`nzcount()` gives the number of stored values, read from the metadata of the
`data` array:

```{r nzcount}
nzcount(seed(X))
nzcount(seed(X)) / length(X)
```

# Subsetting

Subsetting is delayed. Data is read when the result is printed or realized:

```{r subset}
X[1:5, 1:8]
as.matrix(X[c(10, 3, 3), c(100, 1)])
```

Bioconductor usually stores genes as rows and cells as columns, which is the
transpose of AnnData. `t(X)` turns the CSR seed into a CSC seed without
reading any data, and gives a `ZarrSparseMatrix` with genes as rows. Unlike
a delayed transpose, the result is read directly in its new orientation, so
it is as fast to read as `X`:

```{r transpose}
tX <- t(X)
tX
seed(tX)
```

Once a `ZarrSparseMatrix` is subset or modified it becomes an ordinary
`DelayedMatrix`, and `t()` is delayed. To get the fast transpose, transpose
first and subset afterwards, e.g. `t(X)[genes, cells]` rather than
`t(X[cells, genes])`.

# Summaries and block processing

Summaries such as `rowSums()` and `colSums()` are computed block by block, so
only one block is in memory at a time:

```{r sums}
libsize <- rowSums(X)
head(libsize)

gene_mean <- colMeans(X)
head(gene_mean)
```

The block size is set with `setAutoBlockSize()`. A small value forces many
blocks, which shows that the result doesn't depend on it:

```{r blocks}
old <- getAutoBlockSize()
setAutoBlockSize(2000)
all.equal(colSums(X), colSums(as.matrix(X)))
setAutoBlockSize(old)
```

Operations such as normalization and `log1p()` are delayed too. Nothing is
computed until the result is used:

```{r delayed-ops}
logcounts <- log1p(X / libsize * 1e4)
logcounts
showtree(logcounts)
```

`blockApply()` runs your own function on each block. Here, the number of
nonzero values per block of rows:

```{r blockApply}
grid <- rowAutoGrid(X, nrow=50)
unlist(blockApply(X, function(block) nzcount(block), grid=grid,
                  as.sparse=TRUE))
```

# Converting to in-memory matrices

`as()` loads the matrix into memory as any sparse or dense class:

```{r convert}
m <- as(X, "dgCMatrix")
class(m)

svt <- as(X, "SVT_SparseArray")
class(svt)

dense <- as.matrix(X[1:3, 1:3])
dense
```

# Row and column names

AnnData stores cell and gene names separately (in `obs` and `var`), so the
names aren't in the `X` group. Pass them with the `dimnames` argument:

```{r dimnames}
cells <- sprintf("cell_%03d", seq_len(nrow(X)))
genes <- sprintf("gene_%03d", seq_len(ncol(X)))
X <- ZarrSparseMatrix(store, "X", dimnames=list(cells, genes))
X[1:3, 1:4]
```

# Using a ZarrSparseMatrix in a SingleCellExperiment

A `ZarrSparseMatrix` can be used as an assay, and stays on disk:

```{r sce, eval=requireNamespace("SingleCellExperiment", quietly=TRUE)}
suppressMessages({
library(SingleCellExperiment)
})

counts <- t(X)
sce <- SingleCellExperiment(assays=list(counts=counts))
sce
class(counts(sce))
```

# CSC matrices and overriding the metadata

A CSC matrix (`encoding-type` `csc_matrix`) is read the same way. Selecting
columns of a CSC matrix is cheap, and selecting rows of a CSR matrix is cheap.

If the group has no `shape` or `encoding-type` attribute, give them with
`dim` and `sparse.layout`. For example, reading the CSR `X` above as CSC
with reversed dimensions gives its transpose directly:

```{r override}
Xcsc <- ZarrSparseMatrix(store, "X", dim=rev(dim(X)), sparse.layout="CSC")
seed(Xcsc)
all.equal(as.matrix(Xcsc), t(as.matrix(X)), check.attributes=FALSE)
```

To read an alternative array that shares `indices` and `indptr` with `data`,
pass its name as `subdata`.

# Writing a Zarr store from Python

Use Zarr format 2, because `r Biocpkg("Rarr")` reads Zarr v2 arrays. Recent
versions of anndata warn that the default will change to v3. Setting the
format explicitly keeps your stores readable in R:

```python
import anndata as ad
import scanpy as sc

ad.settings.zarr_write_format = 2

adata = sc.datasets.pbmc3k()
adata.write_zarr("pbmc3k.zarr")
```

Then in R:

```{r pbmc, eval=FALSE}
X <- ZarrSparseMatrix("pbmc3k.zarr", "X")
```
